judge_assessment.explanation: The hard failure is exactly as stated and I confirmed it in the artifact. worksheet.pdf page 2, item 3 reads in full: 'Circle the number that is greater. Then write it on the line. 21 12'. There is no sequence, no gap and nothing misplaced — it is a bare two-number magnitude comparison, and verify.json id 3 confirms the intent (type 'compare', values [21, 12], skill 'compare-and-order-numbers', while every other problem is tagged 'fill-the-missing-number' or 'fix-a-wrong-count'). The judge's supporting observation is also exact: study_guide.pdf page 2 devotes its whole third section, 'Skill 3 — Which Number Is Bigger', to the same off-focus skill, so a third of the guide teaches something the prompt did not ask for. The remaining five problems are on focus and mathematically correct (missing 7; missing 13 and 15; Ben skipped 8; Mia's 15/16 swapped, reordering to 13 14 15 16 17; and the open-response 19), and item 6 is properly declared type 'manual' with a reviewer rubric — the judge's 'otherwise correct' is right. I found two further defects the judge did not reach, recorded below; neither changes the verdict.

strengths_to_preserve: Item 5 is a genuinely different error type from item 4 rather than a restatement of it: Mia's cards read 13 14 16 15 17, so nothing is missing and a child who only asks 'is anything absent?' will pass the row. The key says this out loud — 'This is a misplaced number rather than a missing one — every number is present' — and names the test that works (count the row aloud and stop at the first word that does not match). That pairing is the best thing on the sheet and should survive whatever replaces item 3.

Item 6 is handled correctly end to end: verify.json declares it type 'manual' with a full reviewer rubric, the key prints '(Open response — flagged for manual review.)' with a model child explanation and what to look for, final_response.md names it, and the machine observation records gate_chain_manual_flags true. This is the behaviour the rest of the batch is missing.
Item 1 is verified twice from both directions — 'a + 1' at a=6 and 'b - 1' at b=8 — which mirrors the strategy the study guide teaches (check the other way too) instead of only proving the number.

root_causes.description: The task contract lists verification_targets ['eval', 'compare'] and the author appears to have read that list as a content quota to be satisfied by a problem type rather than as a description of the checking machinery available. A pure magnitude comparison was therefore inserted into a sheet whose focus is 'finding missing or misplaced numbers in a counting sequence', and the study guide grew a matching third section to support it. The 'compare' target was already satisfied on focus by item 5, which uses type 'compare' with order 'asc' to reorder Mia's misplaced cards — so the off-focus item bought nothing.
evidence: evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-004/task.json verification_targets ['eval', 'compare']; the contract's focus is 'finding missing or misplaced numbers in a counting sequence'.
worksheet.pdf item 3: 'Circle the number that is greater. Then write it on the line. 21 12' — no counting sequence is present.
verify.json id 5 is already type 'compare' (order 'asc', values [13,14,16,15,17] -> [13,14,15,16,17]) and is fully on focus, so the compare target did not require item 3.
study_guide.pdf page 2 'Skill 3 — Which Number Is Bigger' with try-it '18 or 11' — one of three sections spent off focus.

root_causes.description: Item 3 prints a response slot the verification does not cover, and then the bank hides that fact. The worksheet tells the child to 'write it on the line', i.e. to write the numeral 21, but verify.json id 3 checks the relation '>' — a different object in a different form. Because '>' is a string sympify cannot parse, the Quick Answers bank prints '3. —', so the one thing the child writes is absent from the bank entirely, and it sits beside '6. —', which is the genuine manual item. In this key the two meanings of the em dash appear two rows apart.
evidence: answer_key.pdf Quick Answers: '3. —' (verified compare '>') and '6. —' (type 'manual') print identically.
worksheet.pdf item 3 instructs 'Then write it on the line', whose answer is the numeral 21; verify.json id 3 expected is the relation '>'.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py _fmt returns '---' for a string sympify rejects, and render_entry returns the same '---' for a manual-only problem.
scripts/verify.py coverage gate (the 'Coverage gap' block near line 2015) only requires one check per problem id, so a printed slot in a different form than the check passes silently.

improvements.title: Never add an off-focus problem to satisfy a verification_targets entry
improvements.proposed_change: State plainly in SKILL.md (and in references/problem-library.md's reframing section) that a task contract's verification_targets names the CHECKING types that are available, never a content quota: if the focus cannot be expressed with a listed type, reframe the focus problem into that type instead of adding a new problem outside the focus. Give the worked example from this case — an out-of-order counting sequence IS a 'compare' with order 'asc' (item 5 already does it), so a bare magnitude comparison was never needed. Then make it mechanical: require verify.json's top-level 'facets' list to be present, require every problem's 'skill'/'facet' to be a member of it, and have tests/check_facet_coverage.py fail on a problem whose skill is outside the declared facet plan. curr-004's verify.json declares no 'facets' key at all, which is how a lone 'compare-and-order-numbers' problem sat unnoticed among five 'fill-the-missing-number' / 'fix-a-wrong-count' items.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture verify JSON declaring facets ['fill-the-missing-number', 'fix-a-wrong-count'] with one problem tagged skill 'compare-and-order-numbers'; assert tests/check_facet_coverage.py exits non-zero and names the stray skill. Add a second fixture with no top-level 'facets' key at all and assert verify.py fails asking for the facet plan. Both fixtures pass today (curr-004 built green with exactly this shape), so both assertions fail before the fix and pass after.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes the mechanism behind this run's only hard failure in the batch: an off-focus problem can no longer be smuggled in under a verification target, and the facet plan becomes a declared contract the build checks rather than an optional annotation.
improvements.risk: Low to medium. Making 'facets' mandatory is a schema change that would fail existing verify JSONs that omit it — stage it as a warning for one run, then promote to exit 1. The skill-membership check is exact string matching, so it needs a clear error message telling the author to either rename the skill or extend the plan.

improvements.title: Quick Answers must typeset a verified relation instead of the manual-only em dash
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, handle relation expecteds before the sympify fallback in _fmt: when a problem entry is type 'compare' with order 'relation', map the expected string '<', '>', '=', '<=', '>=', '!=' onto its LaTeX glyph ($<$, $>$, $=$, $\le$, $\ge$, $\ne$) and, where the compare 'values' are literals, print the resolved comparison (e.g. '$12 < 15$') so the bank row carries the same information as the worked solution. Reserve '---' exclusively for problems whose only entries are type 'manual', and add a build warning when _fmt would emit '---' for a non-manual entry, so a future silent drop is loud. Keep this fix separate from the sympify-sandbox fix (quick-answers-must-not-typeset-python-builtins) — that one must REJECT a non-mathematical object, this one must RENDER a relation.
improvements.regression_test: Add to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py a fixture verify JSON holding one {'id':1,'type':'compare','order':'relation','expected':'<'} entry and one {'id':2,'type':'manual','desc':...} entry, then assert the generated bank contains a typeset '<' on row 1 and '---' on row 2, and that row 1 is not '---'. Today row 1 renders '---' (sympify('<') raises SympifyError and _fmt falls through), so the assertion fails before the fix and passes after. Cases in this run that the test reproduces: curr-004 problem 3, whose '—' sits three rows from problem 6's genuine manual '—'.
improvements.expected_impact: Every verified inequality/equality answer becomes visible in the answer key's fast-checking bank, and the em dash regains its single meaning ('nobody machine-checked this'), so a grader can tell a verified relation from a genuine manual item at a glance.
improvements.risk: Low. The change is confined to formatting one expected value; existing numeric, list and dict rows are untouched. The only visible difference is that rows previously blank now print a glyph, which can widen a bank column and re-flow column_count — worth asserting the column arithmetic in the same test.

improvements.title: Coverage gate must count printed answer slots, not problem ids
improvements.proposed_change: scripts/verify.py's coverage gate currently only requires that every id in 1..problem_count has at least one check (see the 'Coverage gap' block near line 2015), which is why a problem printing two blanks passes with one entry. Add a slot-count gate: have tests/check_answer_line.py (it already segments the worksheet .tex by problem via _tex_segments) count the response slots inside each problem's span — \ansblank, \answerline/\ansline, standalone \underline{\hspace{...}} blanks, and lettered parts '(a)'/'(b)' — and fail the build when a problem's slot count exceeds the number of verify entries carrying that id, naming the uncovered slot. Allow an explicit per-problem opt-out field ("slots": N) for the case where two blanks genuinely hold one answer (a restated equation), so the gate is precise rather than merely noisy. State the rule in SKILL.md beside the existing coverage paragraph: one verify entry per printed response, not per problem number. In this case the uncovered slot is item 3's 'write it on the line' (the numeral 21), which verify.json id 3 does not check — it checks the relation '>' instead.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture worksheet .tex with a single problem printing '$10 + \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}} = \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}$' and a verify JSON with one eval entry for that id; assert the answer-line gate exits non-zero and names problem 1's second slot. Add the missing entry and assert exit 0. Today the gate passes both, so the first assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes the single largest verification blind spot in the run: any answer the child actually writes down is either machine-checked or explicitly declared manual, and the answer key's bank stops being narrower than the worksheet.
improvements.risk: Medium. Slot detection is heuristic over LaTeX, so it can false-fail sheets that print a blank as scaffolding (a restated equation, a cross-out target). The "slots" opt-out and a fixture suite covering the \ansblank, \answerline and lettered-part shapes keep the false positives bounded; ship the gate as exit 2 (manual review) for one run before making it exit 1 if that risk is judged too high.

case_summary: A correct, kind and well-typeset K/1 counting sheet that fails on task adherence, and the judge's diagnosis is exact. Five of six problems and two-thirds of the study guide are on focus; item 3 ('Circle the number that is greater. 21 12') and study-guide Skill 3 are a magnitude-comparison skill the prompt did not ask for. The most likely cause is that the contract's verification_targets ['eval','compare'] was treated as a content quota, even though item 5's card-reordering already supplies a 'compare' check on focus. Two further defects the judge did not reach: item 3's printed response is the numeral 21 while its verify entry checks the relation '>', and the Quick Answers bank prints that verified relation as '3. —', the same glyph it prints for item 6's genuine manual item. Everything else is strong — the missing-versus-misplaced contrast between items 4 and 5 is genuinely well designed, item 1 is verified from both directions, and item 6 is the batch's only correctly declared open response.
